concerns.message: Acceptance item 2 says every lane starts on the 64-sub-unit grid in the 2–4-tile ring, and every lane sails every 8th heading that points into an open side. The heading test ignores where the lane starts, so most lanes sail past or away from the berth. On the synthetic island (dock (9,7), headings [24,32,40,48,56]), take heading 48 (north) from any ring start in columns 11–13. It sails up the open water east of the island, never enters the 3×3 neighbourhood or the reach, and ends far away. The same happens with heading 32 from starts south of the berth row, and with heading 0 from the west dock (17,21)'s south-west ring, which runs aground on the coast at (17,24). By my count, only starts within about ±1.5 tiles across the line of travel ever approach: roughly 15–25% of lanes. So each dock has on the order of 450 sea starts × 5–7 headings × 3 speeds ≈ 7,000–9,000 lanes, and about 80% never reach an accepted step. Item 2 requires those to be 'an exact hard-coded list keyed by (dock, heading, start, speed)', 'empty or tiny on the real docks', with a reason for each. Across the synthetic island plus eight real docks, that list would run to tens of thousands of entries. The task also forbids inventing a start rule, so the worker cannot filter them out.
concerns.consequence: The worker must either paste a generated list of thousands of entries, which only records whatever the code does and can't be reviewed or explained, or add a start or heading filter the task forbids. Either way the candidate breaks item 2's text and the reviewers block it again: the same outcome as sea-compact-fixes-001's coverage review.

concerns.message: A lane that never moors passes if it 'ends more than 1.5 tiles (Euclidean) from the berth centre'. But 1.5 tiles is the inscribed radius of the 3×3 neighbourhood, so almost any ship that ends that close is on an adjacent tile and already accepted. The check can only ever catch a pinched diagonal. The dead zone this run exists to fix doesn't trip it: a head-on ship stopped by the spur at (21,28) rests at tile (22,29), about 592 sub-units (~2.3 tiles) from dock (23,27). That lane 'ends more than 1.5 tiles away' and passes. It would only show up as one row in the huge exact list, which gets regenerated after the fix anyway.
concerns.consequence: A future edit to the sketch or the rule could reintroduce a spur-type dead zone two rows out, and the sweep would stay green. Item 2's promise that 'a docking dead zone can't hide again' wouldn't hold.

concerns.message: Budget: about 9 docks × ~450 starts × 5–7 headings × 3 speeds ≈ 60–80k lanes. Lanes that never moor run to the step cap (~100 steps), so that is roughly 6–8M `sail` calls plus an oracle call per step. A vitest `expect` and a template-string label on every step would push this past the 30 s limit. The task also never says how many steps a lane runs or when it 'ends'.
concerns.consequence: The unit check could time out or become flaky on the shared machine. A worker might then shorten lanes arbitrarily, which changes which lanes count as never mooring.

concerns.message: Item 3 talks about 'its mirror images at the other three south docks'. The quarter is mirrored in y for Old Stones and Mist Cay, so two of those docks are N-side docks (sideOf), not S. Only Palm Key's (23,27) has land to its west. Editing the quarter sketch fixes all four automatically, but any test written against 'the four S docks' will find two.
concerns.consequence: A worker filtering `side === "S"` covers only two of the four docks in the sweep or the head-on test, or wastes time hunting for S docks that don't exist.

simpler_alternative: Keep the sea-start grid and the terrain-only oracle, but change what a lane that never moors must prove. Make the exact list about places where a ship comes to rest, not about individual lanes. A lane that never reaches an accepted step fails if it ever comes to rest while holding ahead (speed 0, aground) inside the 5×5 tile block around the berth, unless its (dock, rest tile) pair is in an exact hard-coded list. Lanes that sail past without grounding need no list entry; the test just counts and reports them. This list really is tiny, a few tiles per dock, and each entry can be explained: for example, synthetic island (10,5) is the island's east coast, two tiles north of the berth. It also catches the spur dead zone directly: before the fix, (23,27) → rest tile (22,29) appears, and after the fix it is gone. Nothing is filtered by where a lane starts. Run the loop with plain comparisons and raise one expect at the end on the collected failures, to stay under 30 s.
cheap_experiment: About 20 minutes, in a throwaway vitest file or tsx script. Add the adjacent-plus-pinch rule to a local copy of `dockInReach`, then run the ring sweep as item 2 describes on the synthetic island and on the real dock (23,27) at the base commit, with the spur still in place. Sort each lane that never moors into three buckets: (a) the ship's final position is within 1.5 tiles, (b) it comes to rest aground within the 5×5 block, (c) other. Also record the total lane count and the run time. My prediction: thousands of lanes fall in (c), which shows the per-lane exact list is unworkable. On the real dock, the spur lanes land in (b) at rest tile (22,29) and never in (a), which shows the 1.5-tile check misses the dead zone this run exists to fix. If both predictions hold, switch to the rest-tile list before any worker starts.
